lessons.title: PowerShell Remoting for SQL Server
lessons.chapterTitle: PowerShell for DBAs, Beyond the Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Install the dbatools module (Install-Module dbatools -Scope CurrentUser), then run Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance against your own SQL Server lab instance to confirm it returns real database objects. Separately, set up PowerShell Remoting (Enable-PSRemoting) between two machines (or two VMs) if available, and run the same dbatools command against a remote instance through Invoke-Command.
slots.deliverable: The console output of Get-DbaDatabase run against your lab instance, plus confirmation (output or screenshot) that the same command ran successfully through PowerShell Remoting against a remote session.

lessons.title: Working With SQL Server via SMO
lessons.chapterTitle: PowerShell for DBAs, Beyond the Basics

lessons.title: Scripting Patterns for DBA Work
lessons.chapterTitle: PowerShell for DBAs, Beyond the Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short PowerShell script using raw SMO ($srv = New-Object Microsoft.SqlServer.Management.Smo.Server 'SQLInstance') to list every database and its recovery model, without dbatools, to see what dbatools is actually wrapping underneath. Then refactor that script using at least 2 real scripting patterns from the lesson — parameterizing the instance name and splatting parameters into a function — so the same logic can run against any instance passed in.
slots.deliverable: Two versions of the same script — raw SMO and the refactored, parameterized version — saved side by side so the improvement is visible.

lessons.title: Error Handling in DBA Scripts
lessons.chapterTitle: PowerShell for DBAs, Beyond the Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Take the parameterized script from the previous slot and wrap its risky operations (the SMO connection, any file path access) in try/catch blocks that write a clear error message and exit cleanly instead of showing a raw .NET exception, then deliberately point it at a nonexistent instance name to confirm the error handling catches it gracefully.
slots.deliverable: The updated script with try/catch error handling, plus output showing the clean error message it produces when pointed at a bad instance name instead of a raw exception.

slots.practicalActivity: Using dbatools, run Backup-DbaDatabase -Type Full against a lab database with -CompressBackup and -Checksum, then build a short health-check script combining Test-DbaLastBackup, a free-disk-space check (Get-DbaDiskSpace), and a quick SQL Agent job-failure check (Get-DbaAgentJob | Where-Object LastRunOutcome -eq 'Failed'). Finally, run dbatools' index/statistics maintenance cmdlet against the same lab database and confirm it completes without error.
slots.deliverable: Console output from the backup command, the combined health-check script with output from a real run, and confirmation the index/stats maintenance cmdlet completed successfully.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short security-audit script using a dbatools cmdlet like Get-DbaUserPermission or Get-DbaLogin to list every login on your lab instance and flag any with sysadmin that you don't recognize as legitimate. Register that script and the previous slot's backup script as two separate scheduled tasks (Windows Task Scheduler or Register-ScheduledJob), then deliberately break one script (point it at a bad instance) and add try/catch error handling so the scheduled run fails loud, with a clear logged message, instead of silently.
slots.deliverable: The security-audit script's output flagging logins, screenshots of both scripts registered as scheduled tasks, and a log entry showing the deliberately-broken run failing with a clear error message instead of a silent failure.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a new SQL Server Database Project in SSDT (or Azure Data Studio's Database Projects extension) from your lab database using the Import wizard, then run Schema Compare between that project and the live database after making one small change directly in the database (e.g. add a column) to see the drift Schema Compare detects.
slots.deliverable: The generated .sqlproj with its imported schema objects, plus a Schema Compare report showing the one deliberate drift introduced.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a stored procedure and a view to the database project from the previous slot, commit the whole project to a new Git repository, then create a feature branch, modify the stored procedure on that branch only, and merge it back to main — practicing the same branch-per-change workflow a real database team uses for schema code.
slots.deliverable: A Git repository with the committed database project, a merged feature branch's commit history showing the stored procedure change, and the final merged .sql file.

slots.practicalActivity: Open a pull request (on GitHub, Azure DevOps, or another Git host) for one more schema change to the database project, and review it against a real database code-review checklist: does it include a rollback path, does it avoid a blocking schema change on a large table, is naming consistent with the rest of the project. Leave at least 2 concrete review comments on your own PR before merging.
slots.deliverable: A pull request with at least 2 substantive review comments addressing rollback safety and naming consistency, then merged.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the database project with msbuild (or SSDT's Build command) to produce a .dacpac, then deploy it to a second, separate lab database using SqlPackage.exe /Action:Publish, confirming SqlPackage generates and runs the correct ALTER/CREATE diff automatically rather than it being hand-written.
slots.deliverable: The generated .dacpac file plus the SqlPackage.exe publish command output confirming the diff was deployed to the target database.

lessons.title: Testing Database Changes in a Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: As an alternative to the DACPAC approach, write 2 small, ordered migration scripts (0001_create_table.sql, 0002_add_column.sql) and a short PowerShell runner that tracks which have already applied against a target database in a tracking table, then apply both to a fresh lab database. Add a simple automated test step (a tSQLt test or a plain T-SQL assertion query) that confirms the new column exists and fails loudly if it doesn't.
slots.deliverable: The 2 migration scripts, the tracking-table runner script, and a test script that passes against the migrated database and fails against an un-migrated one.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the rollback script for the migration applied in the previous slot (e.g. DROP the added column, delete the tracking-table row) and run it to confirm the database returns to its prior state. Then assemble everything from this chapter into one real end-to-end pipeline definition (an azure-pipelines.yml or GitHub Actions workflow) that builds the DACPAC, runs SqlPackage publish against a test database, and runs the test script as a pipeline step.
slots.deliverable: The rollback script with confirmed output, plus a working pipeline YAML file with build, deploy, and test stages, and a log of it running end to end.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a minimal Bicep or ARM template (or a docker-compose.yml defining a SQL Server container, if working fully on-prem) that provisions a SQL Server instance as code, and deploy it, confirming the same definition could be redeployed identically to a second environment.
slots.deliverable: The IaC definition file (Bicep/ARM or docker-compose.yml) plus confirmation it successfully provisioned a working SQL Server instance.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend the IaC definition from the previous slot (or add a companion dbatools script using Get-DbaSpConfigure/Set-DbaSpConfigure) to set server configuration values as code — max degree of parallelism, cost threshold for parallelism — rather than by hand in SSMS. Deploy the same configuration to two separate lab instances and run a comparison script against both to confirm they now match.
slots.deliverable: The configuration-as-code script plus a side-by-side Get-DbaSpConfigure comparison confirming both environments now have matching settings.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one combined script that calls the IaC deployment (Bicep/ARM deployment command or docker-compose up) and then immediately runs a dbatools post-provisioning configuration step against the newly created instance (setting MAXDOP, creating a standard login, applying the configuration-as-code from the previous slot) — so provisioning and configuration happen as one automated sequence instead of two manual steps.
slots.deliverable: One combined script (or two scripts called from a single wrapper) that provisions and configures a SQL Server instance end to end with a single invocation, plus its console output.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a PowerShell script that checks a real condition on your lab instance (a failed Agent job via Get-DbaAgentJob, or free disk space below a threshold via Get-DbaDiskSpace) and, when the condition is true, sends a notification — a real email via Send-MailMessage/a mail API, or a real webhook POST to a Slack or Microsoft Teams incoming webhook URL.
slots.deliverable: The alerting script plus confirmation (a received email, Slack message, or Teams message) that the notification actually arrived when the condition was triggered.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a simple custom monitoring dashboard from script output — a PowerShell-generated HTML report (ConvertTo-Html) combining 3-4 dbatools health metrics. Then extend the alerting script from the previous slot so that when the condition fires, it also creates a real incident ticket via an API call (or, with no ticketing system available, writes a structured incident record to a file/table that mimics one).
slots.deliverable: The generated HTML dashboard output showing real metrics, plus confirmation an incident record was created (ticket, or structured file entry) when the alert condition fired.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the alerting script from two slots ago and add at least one alert-fatigue-reduction technique from the lesson — a cooldown/suppression window so the same alert doesn't fire again within N minutes, or a severity threshold that only pages for the worst cases while logging the rest quietly — then deliberately trigger the condition twice in quick succession to confirm the second alert is suppressed or downgraded as designed.
slots.deliverable: The updated alerting script with the suppression/severity logic, plus a log showing the first alert firing normally and the second being suppressed or downgraded.

lessons.title: What DevOps Actually Changes for a DBA

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page reflection comparing how you, personally, would have handled a schema change request before this course (the 'email me a .sql file' pattern) versus the CI/CD pipeline built in Chapter 4, specifically naming what changes about your working relationship with developers — shared repo, pull requests, automated tests — versus the old email-based handoff.
slots.deliverable: A one-page before/after reflection naming at least 3 concrete workflow changes in how you'd now work with a development team.

slots.practicalActivity: Identify one schema-change risk in your own pipeline (Chapter 4) that could be caught earlier — e.g. a missing-index check or a destructive-change linter running at pull-request time instead of after deployment — and add that check as an actual pipeline step. Then write a blameless postmortem for a realistic incident (use a 'forgot a backup before a long weekend' scenario as the subject) following a real blameless-postmortem structure: timeline, contributing factors, and action items, with zero individual blame language.
slots.deliverable: The added shift-left pipeline check (its YAML/script step) plus a written blameless postmortem document with timeline, contributing factors, and action items.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Automate a DBA's Entire Routine

slots.practicalActivity: Following the Meridian Outfitters capstone scenario, build the MeridianDBAOps automation suite's first two scripts for real: Invoke-MeridianBackups.ps1 (using Backup-DbaDatabase with the full/differential/log cadence from Chapter 2) and Invoke-MeridianHealthCheck.ps1 (combining the health-check pattern from Chapter 2), each targeting a lab instance standing in for MERSQLPRD01.
slots.deliverable: The two working scripts (Invoke-MeridianBackups.ps1, Invoke-MeridianHealthCheck.ps1) plus console output from a real run of each against your lab instance.

lessons.title: Capstone: Add CI/CD for a Database Change

slots.practicalActivity: Continuing the capstone, create the MeridianCommerce.sqlproj database project and a pipeline (azure-pipelines.yml or equivalent) that builds and deploys a schema change via SqlPackage, reusing the Chapter 4 pattern. Then add Send-MeridianAlert.ps1, a shared alerting helper reusing the Chapter 6 pattern, and wire it into the health-check script so a failed check actually sends a notification.
slots.deliverable: The MeridianCommerce.sqlproj with a working deploy pipeline, plus Send-MeridianAlert.ps1 wired into the health check with confirmation an alert fires on a deliberately failed check.

slots.practicalActivity: Prepare and actually deliver (to a peer, mentor, or recorded for yourself) a 5-minute walkthrough of the complete MeridianDBAOps suite as if presenting to Priya's manager: what manual habit each script eliminates, a live or screen-recorded demo of one script running, and the measurable time/risk saved. Then write a short course wrap-up noting which of the 8 chapters' techniques you're most likely to use in your next real DBA role.
slots.deliverable: A 5-minute presentation (delivered live, recorded, or written as speaker notes) covering all 3 automated habits, plus a short personal wrap-up note.

slots.practicalActivity: Final capstone integration lab: run the complete MeridianDBAOps suite end to end in one sitting, in the order Priya would actually need it on a real morning — Invoke-MeridianHealthCheck.ps1 first, then Invoke-MeridianBackups.ps1, confirm Send-MeridianAlert.ps1 fires correctly if a check is deliberately broken, and finally trigger the CI/CD pipeline with one more small schema change — so scripts, pipeline, and alerting all run together as a single integrated toolkit rather than three separate demos.
slots.deliverable: A single end-to-end run log showing the health check, backup, alert, and pipeline deployment all executing successfully in sequence against the same lab environment.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can automate a DBA's full routine with PowerShell and dbatools, put database schema changes under source control with a working CI/CD pipeline, provision and configure SQL Server as code, and build automated monitoring and alerting -- the complete DevOps toolkit a working DBA uses to stop doing backups, health checks, and deployments by hand.
